office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: Jennings County School Corporation, based in North Vernon, serves Jennings County with six elementary schools (Brush Creek, Graham Creek, Hayden, North Vernon, Sand Creek and Scipio), Jennings County Middle School, Jennings County High School, an educational center and Panther Online Academy [24]. Federal data list 3,800 students in 2024-25 [25]; Superintendent Dr. Nicole Johnson reported enrollment of 3,659 in February 2025 and 3,486 in August 2026 [26, 27].

The board has seven members serving four-year terms [28, 29, 30]. State election results show the seats are elected as District 1, District 2 and District 3 (one member each, last elected in 2024), District 4 (two members) and At Large (two members) [31, 32, 33]. The board elected Dr. Amy Pettit president in January 2026; the district lists Cheryl Miller as vice president and Pat Sullivan as secretary [34, 30].

Seat counts differ from the state list: the state's 2026 list shows 'vote for 1' in both the District 4 and At Large races [6], but in 2018 the District 4 race and in 2022 both the District 4 race and the At Large race each elected two members, which is the cycle on the ballot again in 2026 [31, 32]. (The 2022 state results label the District 4 race only as 'School Board'.) If two seats are filled in each race, the two District 4 candidates would both be elected and voters would pick two of the four At Large candidates. Voters should check their ballot for the number to vote for.

Who holds the seats now: Amy Pettit and Mary Lynn Whitcomb won the two District 4 seats in 2022 (3,685 and 3,561 votes; Anna Morgan had 3,498), and both are running again [32, 6]. Pettit was first elected in District 4 in 2018 [31]. Cheryl L. Miller and Travis D. Shepherd won the two At Large seats in 2022 [32]. Shepherd, first elected at large in 2018, is running again; Miller is not on the 2026 list [31, 6].

Other members: Chelsea Morrison (District 1) and Patrick Sullivan (District 3) were elected in 2024 [33]. The board appointed Curt Nieman in June 2025 to the District 2 seat, whose term runs through Dec. 31, 2028, choosing him after interviews scored with a rubric [35].

Enrollment decline and cost cutting: at a December 2025 work session Johnson said the district had lost an average of 100 students a year for 15 years, that a demographer projects continued decline over the next seven years, and that 'we will have to continue with cost containment' given enrollment loss and what she called flat-lined state funding [36]. In February 2026 she said the district would absorb 13 certified positions, including moving from building-level instructional coaches to three district-wide coaches, cut five classified positions, and offer early-retirement incentives, and that it did not expect a reduction in force for certified staff [37].

Facility, capacity and enrollment study: in February 2026 Johnson said the district would study redistricting and school capacity, would not close a school for 2026-27, but that a closure 'would be a possibility in the future' if enrollment kept falling [37]. On April 23, 2026 the board voted 7-0 to hire Comprehensive Systems for Support for Schools, LLC to review facilities and resources against enrollment, including 'possible recommended action steps such as redistricting or school closure(s)' [38]. At the Sept. 17, 2026 meeting Johnson said no decisions had been made and Pettit encouraged community involvement [39]. The district posts the study and its cost-reduction documents online [40].

Budget and property taxes: the board heard a presentation on state property-tax changes and their effect on schools from Policy Analytics in July 2025 [41]. The Plain Dealer-Sun reported that in October 2026 Johnson tied the study to 'Senate Bill One's effects' combined with enrollment loss [42]. The 2027 budget notice lists a $35 million Education Fund, a $15.5 million Operations Fund with a maximum operating levy of $10,736,518 (up 6.01% from the current levy), and an estimated $1,293,100 in property-tax cap credits [43]. Johnson said in August 2026 that the district has no referendums [27]. The 2027 budget, capital projects plan and bus replacement plan were set for adoption Oct. 1, 2026 [44], and the Plain Dealer-Sun reported they were adopted [42].
Pre-K: after the state cut Pre-K voucher funding for 2026-27, the board in February 2026 approved consolidating Pre-K at one site, North Vernon Elementary, with tuition of $150 a week [45, 37].

School safety and facilities: Johnson described three bonds in December 2025, including one for secured entries and safety and one for HVAC work at two elementary schools [36]. In October 2026 the district chose OpenGate weapons-detection systems for its schools, with training set for after fall break, according to the Plain Dealer-Sun [42]. In April 2026 the board approved a facility assessment by Garmann Miller to guide future use of bonds [38].

Academics and planning: Johnson reported a high school graduation rate of 95.93% in January 2026 [46]. The district's new strategic plan, BLUEprint 2030, has five action areas, including academic achievement and fiscal responsibility [38]. The Plain Dealer-Sun reported the board approved an agreement with SOAR for a middle school grant of $600,000 in a planning year and $5 million in each of three later years [42].

Forums and coverage: this guide found no 2026 candidate forum, questionnaire, candidate website or news coverage of the candidates' views for either race. The local paper (the Plain Dealer-Sun) could be searched only in part.

candidates.summary: Incumbent and current board president, first elected in District 4 in 2018 and re-elected in 2022 [31, 32, 34].
background: Board member since winning a District 4 seat in 2018; she placed first in the 2022 District 4 race with 3,685 votes [31, 32].
Elected board president in January 2026 by a 7-0 vote; June 2025 minutes also identify her as board president [34, 35]. Minutes refer to her as Dr. Pettit [36].
path_to_ballot: Listed as Nonpartisan on the state list, which gives a filing date of June 16, 2026 [6].

items: Responding to a public comment about bullying in April 2025, she said the board is 'deeply committed to all Jennings County students' having a safe learning environment, that it takes allegations of bullying 'very seriously,' and urged parents to report concerns to teachers, counselors, administrators, ParentSquare or the anonymous website tool, or to Central Office if a concern is not addressed [47].
At the Sept. 17, 2026 meeting she encouraged the community to stay involved in the facility, capacity and enrollment study, saying the district wants the community's input [39].

on_incumbent: Is a current board member and the board president. No campaign statement from her on the board's record was found.
endorsements_finance: No endorsements or campaign finance reports were found.
gaps: No campaign website, questionnaire, forum remarks or news coverage of the 2026 campaign were found.
Occupation, the field of her doctorate and ties to the schools beyond board service could not be confirmed.
Jennings County campaign finance reports were not found online.

candidates.summary: Incumbent, elected to a District 4 seat in 2022 [32].
background: Won the second of two District 4 seats in 2022 with 3,561 votes, 63 more than Anna Morgan [32].

At board meetings she made the motions to approve a facility assessment by Garmann Miller (April 2026) and the updated personal-communication-device policy for 2026-27 (July 2026), both approved unanimously [38, 48]. She also moved to approve a package of policy updates in March 2026, including the board's revised bylaw on election and eligibility to serve, approved 7-0 [49].

candidates.summary: Incumbent, elected at large in 2018 and re-elected in 2022 [31, 32].
background: Won At Large seats in 2018 and 2022; in 2022 he finished second of six candidates for two seats with 2,563 votes, 43 ahead of Josh Yeager [31, 32].
path_to_ballot: Listed as Nonpartisan on the state list, which gives a filing date of June 8, 2026 [6].

items: In August 2025 he asked whether a stipend for two CDL-program adjunct instructors was for planning or teaching; told it was for planning, he cast the only no vote in a 6-1 approval [50].
In June 2025 he asked for confirmation that the District 2 appointee, Curt Nieman, had scored highest on the interview rubric before the board voted 6-0 to appoint him [35].
In January 2026 he asked whether a buy-back payment is always required when schools leave the Southeastern Career Center cooperative; the board then approved the related resolution 7-0 [46].
At an August 2025 enrollment update he asked whether an increase in kindergarten numbers was across the board; Johnson said she would provide the detail [51].
When the board approved a new personal-communication-device policy for 2026-27 in July 2026, he asked whether there were plans for when the rule is broken; Johnson said there are procedures [48].
